summary: A description of the UCSD Computer Center's FTP server, which required a valid user code and password because the center charged for its services. It lists the FTP commands it accepted, and notes that each transfer ran as a separately billed job on its B6700 computer. It follows the FTP of RFC 354 with noted exceptions.

eli5.summary: A guide to how one computer center let people send files, with sign-in required because it charged money.

questions: what was the ucsd-cc ftp server
how did early ftp servers handle billing
subtitle: Describing how a computer center's file transfer service worked on a B6700.

tldr.problem: The UCSD Computer Center was a shared facility that needed to charge users for computing resources. Early FTP servers did not require authentication or account management, so the center needed a way to track which users accessed it and bill them accordingly.
tldr.mechanism: The UCSD server requires users to log in with a valid user code and password before any file transfer commands are accepted. Each transfer runs as a separate process on the B6700 computer and is billed separately by the accounting system.
tldr.outcome: The server supported standard FTP operations like RETR and STOR but also extended the protocol with special commands like ALLO to set file attributes (record size, storage medium, output type) for B6700 files.

today: RFC 532 documents the UCSD Computer Center's early FTP implementation in 1973. It shows how an early computing facility integrated FTP with its mainframe accounting system and resource management practices.

sections.title: A Billing-Aware FTP Server
sections.content:
The UCSD Computer Center operated as a fee-for-service facility. Unlike public FTP servers, it required every user to authenticate with a valid user code and password before accepting any file transfer commands. Once authenticated, a user could access files stored on disk or on tape, and each file transfer was handled as a separate process on the B6700 computer, charged separately to that user's account.

The implementation followed RFC 354 (the FTP specification from July 1972) with noted exceptions. The design allowed the center to bill users for processor time, I/O, core memory, and tape storage consumed by each transfer.
sections.eli5: The place had a front desk. You had to show your membership card and password before anyone would send you a file.

sections.title: Supported Commands and Restrictions
sections.content:
The server accepted most standard FTP commands: USER and PASS for authentication, RETR and STOR for file transfers, TYPE to select ASCII or Image mode, MODE for stream mode, and STRU for file or record structuring. Less common commands like APPE (append) and DELE (delete) were not yet implemented.

The server enforced restrictions on several parameters: byte size was fixed at 8 bits, transfer mode only stream, and a special XLINE command helped transfer text files between systems that did not support record structuring. For record structuring, if an incoming record exceeded the file's maximum record size, the transfer was aborted and the file closed.
sections.eli5: The system said yes to some commands and no to others. Text files could have special line endings, and files could be padded with blanks or zeros if they were too short.

sections.title: File Attributes and B6700 Integration
sections.content:
A unique feature was the ALLO command, used to specify B6700 file attributes such as KIND (TAPE9 or disk), MAXRECSIZE (maximum record length), MYUSE (direction of tape use), and TITLE (file name). These attributes matched those of B6700 "label-equate" cards used in batch job submission, giving remote users control over file characteristics similar to local B6700 users.

When storing to tape, users had to specify MYUSE=OUT. Tape access also required prior arrangements with on-site operators via TELNET to mount the correct tape. The center planned to eventually allow users to communicate directly with operators through FTP itself.
sections.eli5: You could add a tag to say what kind of tape or disk you wanted and how big your records should be, like filling out a form for the computer center staff.

sections.title: File Management and Use
sections.content:
The server allowed users to retrieve existing files or store new ones. If no ALLO command was given before STOR, the file was given the name from the STOR command and received default B6700 file attributes. For other operations like file deletion (DELE) and renaming (RNTO, RNFR), users were directed to log in via TELNET to the CANDE interface and use the LIBMAINT program instead.

Overall, the UCSD server demonstrated how FTP could be extended for a specific computing environment, allowing the center to maintain control over resources while letting remote users transfer files to and from tape and disk storage.
sections.eli5: You could send and get files, but if you wanted to erase or rename them, you had to log in to a different system and use a different tool.

references.text: Merryman, R., "File Transfer Protocol (Revision 4)", RFC 354, July 8, 1972.
